title: Wind speed
text:
Purpose. Characterize Cal-Adapt Analytics Engine 10 m wind speed (wspeed / wspd10mean), 1980–2014, against the quality dimensions fixed in Scope & Definitions. Findings derived here feed the good/bad matrix.
Evaluated against station observations from HDP first, then against CONUS404 and ERA5.

title: Wind speed
section: 1. What the stations can and cannot be
text:
1. What the stations can and cannot be
Stations are the primary reference, not a common frame in the gridding sense, and the difference matters:

They are points. A station samples one spot; a LOCA2/WRF cell averages 9 km² and an ERA5 cell ~950 km². Part of every model–station difference is this footprint mismatch and cannot be removed.
They do not cover the ocean, and they are sparse above 2,000 m, exactly where §7 shows the products and ERA5 diverge most.

So a gridded comparison still earns its place, for spatial and seasonal structure and for the ocean control. That is what §7 uses ERA5 for.

title: Wind speed
text:
9. Caveats

On the observational reference

Only airports are unobstructed. Every other class confounds model error with shelter (§2)..
Footprint. A station is a point; a LOCA2 cell averages 9 km² and an ERA5 cell ~950 km². Part of §2’s “only a third within ±10 %” is this and cannot be removed.
A calm floor. 13.2 % of hourly observations are exactly zero, the ASOS/AWOS sub-3-kt convention. No model reproduces it, so observed means are biased low and every ratio here is slightly generous to the model.
Reporting quantisation. Harmless for means; relevant to §5’s Weibull fits and quantile ratios.
338 of 1,207 stations screened out, 292 for records under 60 months. The retained 869 are not a random sample of the archive.
Coverage gaps. No ocean stations, and few unobstructed high-terrain stations, the Sierra has 11 airports against 73 RAWS. The products are least verifiable exactly where §7 shows they diverge most from ERA5.



On what is not measured

No uncertainty. Every result is a median with no bootstrap, no confidence interval, no effective sample size for autocorrelated series.
No hourly data in this analysis, so no diurnal analysis. It is not settled how valid a model-against-hourly-station comparison would be.
Historical only. No check that skill is stationary under warming.

title: Scope & Definitions
text: Purpose. Set the boundaries and the method before characterization starts, so results are comparable across variables and the work is repeatable. Items marked [CONFIRM in review] / [FILL] are decisions for the science team; everything else is drawn from the lit-review database and flagged with source IDs.

title: Scope & Definitions
text:
1. Datasets in scope
The two downscaling paths treat most variables fundamentally differently, and the difference is the single most useful thing to know about them.

WRF 3 km CA convection-permitting (d03) : the dynamical path, and the one that physically simulates the atmosphere. Native hourly output; resolves terrain-driven and mesoscale flow. (R12, R19; R04 validation.)
LOCA2 CA hybrid, 3 km : the statistical/hybrid downscaling. Trained to reproduce an observational target, so it inherits that target’s spatial structure rather than generating its own.

[CONFIRM in review] exact cadcat versions/paths, and whether 9 km WUS-D3 is in scope.






Not every variable is downscaled at parity. Wind is not statistically downscaled in LOCA2 the way temperature and precipitation are (R02).

Observations first. A ratio against a coarse reanalysis measures a distance, not an error: at 0.25° (~31 km) a reanalysis cannot represent a 3 km ridge–valley contrast, so disagreement over terrain is expected and is not by itself evidence against either side.
The reanalysis earns its place through coverage. It is the only field that is complete and uniform, which makes it the only one that can supply a control region, somewhere the mechanism under test should switch off. For wind that is the ocean, where a resolution effect must vanish and a calibration error must not.






Station siting is the limiting factor, and it is not standardised. Instrument height usually is. Where the instrument stands is not, and that difference is a large source of scatter in every station comparison. Open (exposed) sites will behave differently from sheltered ones.

title: Scope & Definitions
text:
5. Choosing the metric
The metric is not universal. Decide it before any comparison is run and state it on the characterization page. Wind speed is an unbounded variable, while relative humidity is bounded between 0 and 100 %.
A ratio is meaningless for a bounded variable: where observed RH is 90 %, no model can score above 1.11 however wrong it is, so a map of RH ratio is largely a map of where the observations are high.
Beyond a bias, two diagnostics have proved decisive and are now standard:
Distribution analysis examines the overall shape of the variable’s distribution, and a quantile comparison (Q–Q against observations). A straight line through the origin means the departure is affine, a shift and a stretch, and a simple correction is the right functional form. Curvature means it is not.

text:
7. Known issues to carry in from the start

Absolute bias and its sensitivity to model configuration.
Complex terrain and coastal transitions, where both model error and observational reference are worst (R18).
The sparse-California-reference problem for anything trained on observations (DQ9; R16).
Robustness of projected changes for maxima vs means (DQ6); spatial consistency of trends across GWLs (DQ7).


Sources: R02, R04, R12, R16, R18, R19; open questions DQ6, DQ7, DQ9. Full entries on the References page.

text:
Purpose. Characterize the cadcat archive itself, not what the data say, but whether the metadata describing them is correct, complete, and consistent with Cal-Adapt’s own published documentation.
Produced by cadcat_qc, run over WRF and LOCA2-Hybrid across all domains (d01/d02/d03) and all temporal resolutions (1hr/day/mon/yrmax).

Non-compliant on both: it needs to be fixed at the source
Neither the store nor the delivered product meets the documented requirement. Sixty rows, dominated by self-description: empty global attributes, missing long_name, missing Conventions.






wind.rotation.undeclared is the one with analytical consequences. Wind components must declare their reference frame, and grid-relative and earth-relative are not interchangeable. The difference is a rotation by the map projection’s convergence angle, up to several degrees across the domain. uas declares no frame, so a consumer cannot confirm which it has. See §4.





Introduced by climakitae: the store is fine
The published store satisfies the requirement; what users receive does not. Every AE user is affected regardless of the store’s state, and fixing the store would change nothing.
The largest is dataset.aggregated (37 rows): a query pinning every available facet still returns several stores combined rather than one published dataset. Time alignment across members can then silently drop dates that any one member lacks.


Repaired by climakitae: still a defect, but mitigated
crs.spatial_ref.missing, 40 rows. LOCA2 stores should carry a spatial_ref coordinate holding the WGS84 definition; they do not, and climakitae attaches one on read.
Invisible to AE users, and still worth fixing: it affects anyone reading the Zarr directly, and it depends on that repair continuing to exist.

Two codes account for 208 of the 276 errors, and both are on WRF’s u10/v10.
catalog.path.staging_prefix: the store is served from a tmp prefix rather than its canonical location. Data under a staging prefix carries no persistence guarantee, so anything pinned to that path can vanish without notice.
catalog.path.variable_qualifier_dropped: the store holds u10_earth but the catalog indexes it as u10. The _earth qualifier means earth-relative; WRF’s native u10/v10 are grid-relative. A user querying u10 receives a rotated field and the catalog does not say so.

title: Catalog audit
text:
4. What this means for wind
Three audit findings land directly on the wind speed characterization:
The wind components are the worst-affected variables in the archive. u10 and v10 at every domain carry both ERROR codes (32 to 36 findings each), more than any other dataset.
The reference frame is unresolved in two directions at once. The catalog drops the _earth qualifier, so a query for u10 may return an earth-relative field indexed as if it were grid-relative; and uas declares no frame at all, so neither can be confirmed from the file. The wind review’s §10 notes that no wind direction is published in the analysed archive.
A staging prefix is not a stable citation. Anything pinning a u10 path from the catalog is pinning a location with no persistence guarantee.






None of this changes the wind speed results. wspd10mean and wspeed are scalar speeds and rotation-invariant, and the analysis sampled stores rather than citing paths. It changes what a user should do with the component variables.

title: Catalog audit
text:
6. What to do with this
For the catalog maintainers, in order of user impact:

u10/v10 off the staging prefix, and either index the _earth qualifier or publish the grid-relative field the catalog claims. 208 of 276 errors.
Declare the wind reference frame in the component variables’ attributes.
Document dew_point, effective_temp_index, and rh at 1hr (or remove them from the catalog). Published-but-undocumented is (in my opinion)the worst of the three states.
Fill the empty global attributes. A reader cannot tell an empty value from an unanswered question.

For this pillar: the audit runs in seconds at catalog level and returns CI-friendly exit codes (0 clean, 1 warnings, 2 errors). Running it on a schedule would catch a regression when it is introduced rather than at the next manual audit.

title: Catalog audit
text:
Method
Metadata is a property of (activity_id, institution_id, table_id, grid_label, variable_id) rather than of which GCM or member produced the run, so the sweep opens one store per unique facet combination and records how many stores each sample stands for. experiment_id is included because expected start and end years are per-experiment.
Checks cover: catalog-row validity against the documented vocabularies; variable presence, units and long_name; a three-tier unit comparison (alias table, accepted physical restatements, then a dimensional check, K versus degC stays a mismatch because the offset matters); global attributes against the recommended six; CRS per the documented split; coordinates, grid spacing against the nominal 45/9/3 km; time decoding, extent, cadence, monotonicity and per-model leap-day rules; and Zarr store structure.
Expectations live in one place (standards.py) and the checks read from it rather than hard-coding thresholds.
Full findings: data/audit/all_findings.csv (1,961 rows) and data/audit/reconciliation.csv.

title: Variable Cards
text:
wspeed — 10 m wind speed (scalar)






Definition. Scalar daily-mean 10 m wind speed: the hourly wind speeds are averaged to daily. It is not the magnitude of the daily-mean vector components.










Datasets
LOCA2 CA hybrid (3 km); WRF (WUS-D3) also carries native wind


Units
m/s


Temporal
daily


Type
separately downscaled, independently validated scalar field


Provenance
GCM -> LOCA2 hybrid downscaling (WRF pattern library) -> wspeed


Use wspeed for
wind-speed magnitude, directly


Don’t confuse with
uas, vas (vector components) - their magnitude is not equal to wspeed









Known issue — DQ4 (resolved). wspeed and sqrt(uas^2 + vas^2) differ at daily resolution by design. Wind speed (positive-definite) and the vector components (signed) are downscaled and bias-corrected separately, with different extreme-value handling, so the two are not equal and wspeed must not be reconstructed from the daily components. The difference is centred positive (scalar pedestal) with a left-skewed tail from the differing bias-correction of the two distributions. All three fields agree well seasonally. Guidance (Scripps): use the wspeed variable directly. Confirmed R20.



Validated: Scripps CA-hybrid seasonal validation (R04), RMSE ~0.4-0.5%; vs ERA5 1980-2010 head-to-head (Q05, v2): both downscaled products high, timing agrees; LOCA2 +29% is closer than dynamical WRF-GCM +69%; offset worst over flat interior. The earlier PresRat explanation is rejected - origin is upstream of downscaling. Single member; WRF carries a sampling-frequency caveat
Evidence: R04, R15, Q03, R20, Q05
Source: D. Pierce (Scripps), personal communication, August 2026 [confirm exact date] — see R20.
Status: Confirmed (Scripps, R20)

title: Provenance
text:
The shared backbone
Every variable follows the same five stages:

Global climate model: CMIP6, SSP3-7.0
Bias correction: differs by path. A priori on the GCM boundary conditions for WRF (some runs only), quantile-preserving and observation-trained for LOCA2
Downscaling: dynamical (WRF, 3 km, hourly) or statistical/hybrid (LOCA2, 3 km)
Cataloguing: cadcat, analysis-ready
AE-side processing : derived variables, indices, localization

What changes per variable is which variables each path publishes, what is derived rather than native, and which gaps attach where.

title: References
text:
Source details

R01 — Is Bias Correction in Dynamical Downscaling Defensible?
Risser et al. 2024 (GRL 51, e2023GL105979) · Peer-reviewed paper · Sec 4
Summary. Tests whether a priori bias correction (APBC) of GCM boundary conditions before dynamical downscaling is justified.
Key findings. APBC adds negligible uncertainty for temperature and precipitation relative to GCM choice and internal variability. Snow projections without APBC are physically unrealistic. Minimally invasive APBC preserves GCM trends at regional scales.
Datasets: WRF (WUS-D3) · Variables: Temperature, precipitation, snow · Methods: A priori bias correction of boundary conditions; comparison of uncertainty sources
Feeds: Phase 2 proposal; Sec 4 methods shortlist; provenance flowchart (pre-downscaling branch)
Relevance: High · Status: To read

Core justification for the APBC step already applied upstream of AE WRF data




R02 — LOCA Version 2 for North America (ca. Jan 2023)
Pierce / Scripps (UCSD) 2023 · Dataset documentation · Sec 0
Summary. Official documentation page for the LOCA2 downscaled dataset.
Key findings. LOCA2 CMIP6 at 6 km, daily Tmin/Tmax/precip 1950-2100, SSP245/370/585, 27 GCMs / 329 members. Humidity in progress. Wind is not statistically downscaled - supports the LOCA2-barely-carries-wind caveat.
Datasets: LOCA2 (NAmer 6 km) · Variables: Tmax, Tmin, precipitation · Methods: LOCA2 statistical downscaling and its bias correction step
Feeds: Per-dataset bias adjustment documentation; variable cards
Relevance: High · Status: To read

Methodology papers are listed in the LOCA bibliography page - chase and add as separate rows




R03 — LOCA2 (CMIP6) Validation and Verification Plots
Pierce / Scripps (UCSD) 2023 · Validation page · Sec 3
Summary. Historical validation plots for LOCA2 against observations.
Key findings. Means, seasonal cycles, percentiles, return values (20-250 yr), wet spells, humidity metrics. Ready-made figure source.
Datasets: LOCA2 (NAmer 6 km) · Variables: Precipitation, Tmin, Tmax, DTR, specific humidity, RH · Methods: Observation-based validation; return value analysis
Feeds: Good/bad matrix; data challenges page; figure source for guidance doc
Relevance: Medium · Status: To read



R04 — California 3 km LOCA2 Hybrid Downscaling Validation Plots
Pierce / Scripps (UCSD) 2023 · Validation page · Sec 1
Summary. Validation plots for the CA 3 km hybrid WRF/LOCA2 product, including winds.
Key findings. Includes 10 m wind validated against observations (seasonal means, percentiles, daily max/min), plus RH and downward shortwave vs GOES. One of the few obs-vs-model wind comparisons available for AE-relevant data.
Datasets: Hybrid WRF/LOCA2 (CA 3 km) · Variables: 10 m wind (uas/vas + speed), RH min/max, specific humidity, rsds, precipitation, Tmin, Tmax · Methods: Observation-based wind validation
Feeds: Wind pilot Sec 3; good/bad matrix; RH report; figure source for guidance doc
Related questions: DQ4
Relevance: High · Status: To read

Highest-value single source for the wind pilot - start here




R05 — Observed humidity trends in dry regions contradict climate models
Simpson et al. 2024 (PNAS 121(1), e2302480120) · Peer-reviewed paper · Sec 1
Summary. Documents the mismatch between observed and modelled humidity trends in arid regions.
Key findings. CMIP6 models fail to reproduce observed drying (negative RH / vapor pressure trends) in arid and semi-arid regions including the SW US. ERA5 shows a much stronger negative RH trend than the GCMs. This is the root paper behind the AE RH concern.
Datasets: CMIP6 GCMs, ERA5 · Variables: RH, vapor pressure · Methods: Linear trend fitting on observed vs modelled RH
Feeds: RH report (core citation); good/bad matrix
Related questions: DQ1, DQ3
Relevance: High · Status: To read

Cited in Q02; Will reproduced its ERA5 trends in Appendix B. Citation verified Jul 2026: the article was published online 26 Dec 2023 but carries a 2 Jan 2024 issue date, so some databases (OSTI, DOE EESM) list it as 2023. The volume is 121, not 120 - the trailing 120 in the DOI is PNAS submission-era numbering, not the volume.




R06 — DRAFT - Data Justification Memo for California’s Fifth Climate Change Assessment: Climate Adjusted Synthetic Relative Humidity Data
Westerling, Baldwin, Romsos & Saah (Pyregence, draft) · Memo · Sec 4
Summary. The Pyregence team’s own justification for replacing downscaled RH with a statistically derived synthetic product, plus full model specification and data access.
Key findings. Motivation: over the 2000-2020 overlap, GCM-simulated RH is significantly wetter than observed, and observed California RH has a declining trend that the simulations do not reproduce - so fire models calibrated on observations project immediately decreasing fire activity regardless of scenario. KEY CLAIM FOR PHASE 2: the authors argue bias correction can adjust modest discrepancies in mean or variance but CANNOT correct differences in long-term trends, which is why they rebuilt RH rather than correcting it. Authors’ own stated limitations: the model omits large-scale atmospheric moisture transport, underestimates wet extremes of daily max RH, and has no dew point representation so max RH never spikes to 100%. They state the impact is muted for fire models because those are most sensitive to daily MINIMUM RH. Model skill: ~66% of variance explained for rmin, ~45% for rmax. Authors explicitly caution other sectors to assess suitability before using it as a replacement.
Datasets: Pyregence synthetic RH; source data = ERA5 WRF (1950-2021), UCLA WRF bias-corrected, LOCA2 · Variables: RH (daily min/max), tmx, tmn, prc, elevation, aspect · Methods: Semiparametric GAM via bam() in R mgcv, with spline-smoothed interaction terms. RH fractions logit-transformed to unbounded variables. Final form: rmin2 ~ s(tmx,tmn,prc) + s(t90,p90) + s(elv,asp) + s(x,y). AIC-based selection on a 1M random subsample of >1bn daily observations. Windspeed and 30/60-day leading averages were tested but not retained. A day-of-year seasonal term was deliberately excluded so seasonality would emerge from the climate data.
Feeds: Phase 2 proposal (the trend-vs-bias-correction claim is directly load-bearing); RH report; data challenges page
Related questions: DQ3, DQ5, DQ8, DQ11
Relevance: High · Status: Read

Obtained Jul 2026, resolves the placeholder. Confirms Q02‘s reading of the input variables exactly. Still does NOT name the observational training dataset, and still documents no held-out validation - ’robust across randomly selected samples’ is a stability check, not an overfitting test. Crucially it documents NO additional bias correction step on the LOCA2 or WRF-ERA5 inputs, so the large LOCA2 bias shift Q02 observed remains unexplained. Data access via ungoliant.ucmerced.edu (era5wrf/, wrf_bc/, loca2/) as Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs. Relevance raised from Medium to High.




R07 — Future humidity trends over the western United States in the CMIP5 global climate models and variable infiltration capacity hydrological modeling system
Pierce, Westerling & Oyler 2013 (HESS 17(5), 1833-1850) · Peer-reviewed paper · Sec 4
Summary. Prior work on deriving humidity for western US climate assessments using the VIC hydrological model.
Key findings. The methodological precedent R06 builds on and cites for its known limitation: like VIC-derived RH, a statistically/hydrologically derived humidity misses the portion of daily variability driven by large-scale atmospheric moisture transport. Establishes that this limitation is long-standing and not unique to the Pyregence approach.
Datasets: CMIP5 GCMs, VIC · Variables: RH, humidity · Methods: VIC hydrological modelling of humidity; CMIP5 humidity trend analysis
Feeds: RH report (background); Phase 2 proposal (prior art on derived-humidity limitations)
Related questions: DQ3, DQ8
Relevance: Medium · Status: To read

Chased from the R06 reference list. Pierce is also the author of R02-R04, so this connects the LOCA2 and Pyregence threads.




R08 — Statistical Downscaling Using Localized Constructed Analogs (LOCA)
Pierce, Cayan & Thrasher 2014 (J. Hydrometeorol. 15, 2558-2585) · Peer-reviewed paper · Sec 4
Summary. The core peer-reviewed description of the LOCA statistical downscaling method that underlies LOCA2.
Key findings. Analog-based downscaling. The LOCA system has two parts: bias correction and the downscaling step. This is the foundational method reference behind R02-R04 and the LOCA2 hybrid.
Datasets: LOCA (CMIP5 origin), applies to LOCA2 · Variables: Temperature, precipitation · Methods: Localized constructed analogs; observationally trained
Feeds: 1a per-dataset bias adjustment documentation; variable cards
Relevance: High · Status: To read

Named by the LOCA bibliography as the primary description of the method.




R09 — Improved Bias Correction Techniques for Hydrological Simulations of Climate Change
Pierce et al. 2015 (J. Hydrometeorol. 16(6), 2421-2442) · Peer-reviewed paper · Sec 4
Summary. The peer-reviewed bias correction method used in LOCA and LOCA2 - the quantile-preserving scheme.
Key findings. This is the actual LOCA bias correction (‘Pierce et al. 2015a’ in the CEC memos): it preserves GCM-predicted trends by quantile. LOAD-BEARING FOR DQ11 - its trend-by-quantile preservation is the direct counter-case to test against the Pyregence memo’s claim that bias correction cannot fix trends.

The standard LOCA BC scheme cited throughout the CEC memos.




R10 — Downscaling humidity with Localized Constructed Analogs (LOCA) over the conterminous United States
Pierce & Cayan 2015 · Peer-reviewed paper · Sec 4
Summary. How humidity specifically is downscaled and bias-corrected within LOCA.
Key findings. The LOCA-side humidity method that sits underneath the RH bias story - relevant to how RH enters LOCA2. Connects the methods thread to the RH cluster (Q01, Q02, Q04, R05, R06).

Summary. Introduces the LOCA2 multi-ensemble-member bias correction scheme.
Key findings. The ‘Pierce et al. 2023’ pooled multi-member BC used in LOCA2: ensemble members are pooled and bias-corrected together to better preserve rare precipitation extremes. This is the specific LOCA2 (vs LOCA1) bias-correction change.

Key findings. Documents the WUS-D3 WRF configuration, GCM selection, data tiers (6-hourly / hourly / daily), and improvements over raw GCMs. The primary WRF dataset reference - the dynamical-downscaling counterpart to R02 for LOCA2. GCM selection explicitly considered surface wind patterns.
Datasets: WRF (WUS-D3); 9 km WUS + 3 km CA · Variables: 21 hourly + 30 daily variables incl. wind · Methods: WRF dynamical downscaling; ERA5-driven configuration (Rahimi et al. 2022)
Feeds: 1a documentation; wind pilot Sec 1; provenance flowchart (WRF branch)
Related questions: DQ4, DQ6, DQ7
Relevance: High · Status: To read

Open data on AWS (registry.opendata.aws/wrf-cmip6). The WRF equivalent of R02.




R13 — Understanding the Cascade: Removing GCM Biases Improves Dynamically Downscaled Climate Projections
Rahimi et al. 2024 (Geophys. Res. Lett. 51(10)) · Peer-reviewed paper · Sec 4
Summary. The a priori bias correction (APBC) method for the WRF downscaling - correcting GCM biases before downscaling.
Key findings. The WRF-side counterpart to LOCA’s Pierce 2015 BC. Applies a priori BC of GCM boundary conditions before dynamical downscaling. Pairs with R01 (Risser ‘Defensible?’), which evaluates whether this exact APBC step is justified. Relevant to DQ11 and Phase 2.
Datasets: WRF (WUS-D3) · Variables: Temperature, precipitation, hydroclimate · Methods: A priori bias correction of GCM boundary conditions before dynamical downscaling
Feeds: 1a documentation; Phase 2 proposal; provenance flowchart (pre-downscaling WRF branch); DQ11
Related questions: DQ11
Relevance: High · Status: To read

R01 evaluates the defensibility of the APBC this paper applies - treat them as a pair.




R14 — Bias Correction in the WRF and LOCA version 2 Projections (Data Adoption Justification Memo, CA 5th Climate Change Assessment)
Pierce, Rahimi, Cayan & Kalansky 2023 (CEC EPC-20-006) · Memo · Sec 4
Summary. The high-level overview memo describing how bias correction is used in BOTH the WRF and LOCA2 products. *** Best single match for the WRF+LOCA2 bias-correction request. ***
Key findings. Explains that WRF and LOCA2 use different BC methods with different goals, and points to the individual product memos for specifics. The natural anchor document for the 1a bias-adjustment documentation deliverable - start here and branch out.
Datasets: WRF, LOCA2 · Variables: All · Methods: Overview: a priori (WRF) vs quantile-preserving (LOCA2) bias correction
Feeds: 1a documentation (anchor); provenance flowchart; guidance doc
Related questions: DQ11
Relevance: High · Status: To read

CEC-adopted grey literature but authoritative. The best starting point for the documentation deliverable.




R15 — LOCA version 2 Hybrid Downscaling (Data Justification Memo)
Pierce, Cayan, Rahimi & Kalansky 2023 (CEC EPC-20-006) · Memo · Sec 0
Summary. Documents the CA 3 km LOCA2-hybrid product - the WRF-pattern-library + LOCA approach that is the actual cadcat CA hybrid data.
Key findings. The hybrid uses a WRF-derived pattern library plus the standard LOCA quantile-preserving BC (Pierce 2015a, = R09). This is the exact product Ana investigated in Q03 for the wspeed vs uas/vas discrepancy - it documents how that product was built.
Datasets: LOCA2 CA hybrid (3 km) · Variables: incl. 10 m wind (uas/vas/wspeed) · Methods: WRF pattern library + LOCA analog + quantile-preserving BC
Feeds: 1a documentation; variable cards; provenance flowchart (hybrid branch); wind pilot
Related questions: DQ4
Relevance: High · Status: To read

Directly relevant to Q03/DQ4 - documents the CA hybrid product where the wind discrepancy appears.




R16 — LOCA Version 2 - Training Data (Data Justification Memo)
Pierce, Rahimi, Iacobellis, Cayan & Kalansky 2023 (CEC EPC-20-006) · Memo · Sec 4
Summary. Documents the observational training/reference data used for LOCA2 bias correction and analog matching.
Key findings. Training data sets the climatology, annual cycle and variability of the downscaled result. Precip = ‘unsplit Livneh’ (Pierce 2021, better extremes than Livneh 2015); temperature = Livneh 2015 extended to 2018 by Lu Su (UCLA). *** Directly answers ‘which observational reference was used’ - feeds Phase 2 reference-dataset scoping. *** Note wind is NOT in the LOCA training data, reinforcing the LOCA-barely-carries-wind caveat.
Datasets: LOCA2; training = unsplit Livneh (precip), Livneh 2015 ext (temp) · Variables: Precipitation, temperature · Methods: Observational training data for BC and the analog library
Feeds: Phase 2 proposal (reference-dataset scoping); 1a documentation
Related questions: DQ9
Relevance: High · Status: To read

The reference-dataset answer for LOCA2; connects to R02.




R17 — Memo on WRF Downscaling with Bias Corrected Boundary Conditions (the four ‘new’ GCMs)
Rahimi, Pierce, Cayan & Kalansky 2024 (CEC EPC-20-006) · Memo · Sec 4
Summary. Documents the a priori bias-corrected boundary-condition WRF runs for four additional GCMs.
Key findings. The applied ‘what we actually ran’ companion to R13 (the Cascade method paper): the second set of WRF runs driven by bias-corrected GCM boundary conditions. Notable cross-over - the LOCA-side Pierce BC is applied to the GCM boundary conditions that then force WRF.
Datasets: WRF (WUS-D3, 2nd set, 4 new GCMs) · Variables: All WRF variables · Methods: A priori bias-corrected GCM boundary conditions feeding WRF
Feeds: 1a documentation; provenance flowchart (WRF a-priori-BC branch)
Related questions: DQ11
Relevance: Medium · Status: To read

Sept 2024 CEC memo (posted 2025).




R18 — Evaluation of the Mountain Hydroclimate across the Western United States in Dynamically Downscaled Climate Models
Adhikari, Geerts, Rahimi-Esfarjani, Smith, Shuman & Schneider 2024 (J. Hydrometeorol. 25(12), 1877-1894) · Peer-reviewed paper · Sec 3
Summary. Evaluates how well the WUS-D3 WRF downscaling reproduces observed hydroclimate over complex terrain in the western US.
Key findings. Evaluates 15 CMIP6 GCMs downscaled to 9 km (WUS-D3) against PRISM, gauge/station data and a snow reanalysis over 1981-2014 for orographic precipitation, surface temperature and SWE, plus ERA5-driven 9 km and 4 km (CONUS404) reconstructions. Perkins skill for precipitation exceeds 0.9 over plains but is lower over mountains. KEY FOR THE PILLAR: it flags that gridded observational estimates in complex terrain are poorly quantified (esp. PRISM precip over mountains) - the reference-data uncertainty problem that complicates bias correction and validation in exactly the terrain where wind is also hardest.
Datasets: WRF WUS-D3 (9 km); ERA5-driven WRF (9 km + CONUS404 4 km) · Variables: Orographic precipitation, surface temperature, SWE · Methods: Perkins skill score vs PRISM, gauge/station data and snow reanalysis; mountains-vs-plains contrast
Feeds: Good/bad matrix (complex-terrain rows); data challenges page; Phase 2 reference-dataset scoping
Related questions: DQ9
Relevance: Medium · Status: To read

WRF WUS-D3 evaluation, not a bias-correction method paper. Rahimi-Esfarjani = Stefan Rahimi (WUS-D3 lead). Its complex-terrain reference-uncertainty finding is the most transferable point for the wind pilot and for reference-dataset choice.




R19 — CMIP6 Downscaling Using WRF (UCLA Alex Hall Research Group project page)
Alex Hall Research Group, UCLA (accessed Jul 2026) · Website · Sec 0
Summary. The source team’s landing page for the WRF dynamical downscaling, with the full simulation matrix and downloadable per-simulation PDFs.
Key findings. Documents the WRF setup: 9 km WUS, 3 km convection-permitting CA and WY, 21 hourly + 30 daily variables, 1980-2100, mostly SSP3-7.0. KEY: the simulation table lists, per GCM/variant, which resolutions exist AND the bias-correction status of each 3 km CA run - labelled ‘only no-bc’, ‘only bc’, or both - and highlights which simulations were used in California’s 5th Climate Change Assessment. This is the authoritative map of which WRF runs are bias-corrected vs not. Frames the data around wildfire / utility use (aridity + windiness, PSPS).
Datasets: WRF WUS-D3 (45 km / 9 km / 3 km CA / 3 km WY), incl. ERA5-driven runs · Variables: 21 hourly + 30 daily WRF variables · Methods: WRF dynamical downscaling; per-simulation a priori bias correction (bc vs no-bc variants)
Feeds: 1a documentation (bc-vs-no-bc per simulation); provenance flowchart; wind pilot use cases
Related questions: DQ11
Relevance: High · Status: To read

Data-access contact: Stefan Rahimi (UCLA). Highlighted rows = used in the CA 5th Climate Change Assessment. The 3 km CA bc/no-bc labels are the key detail - reconcile against which WRF version cadcat/AE actually serves (Q02 Appendix A notes AE uses the non-a-priori-bias-corrected WRF). Living webpage - note the access date.




Q01 — Relative Humidity Sensitivity Analysis: Fosberg Fire Weather Index
Cal-Adapt AE 2025 (update: Nicole, Mar 2026) · Internal doc · Sec 2
Summary. AE sensitivity analysis of how the known RH bias propagates into FFWI.
Key findings. FFWI likely biased low due to the known RH bias in CMIP6 downscaled GCMs. RH trend switches sign around GWL2.5 (interior increases), making FFWI non-monotonic. Preliminary recommendation: caution or do-not-use for FFWI at GWL>=2.5. RH bias adjustment alone may not fix the FFWI trend. FFWI>50 exceedance counts trend downward over time (especially TaiESM). Mean wind speeds decrease mildly statewide.
Datasets: WRF (AE) · Variables: RH, wind speed, air temperature, FFWI · Methods: GWL delta signal analysis; FFWI decomposition by calculation step; exceedance counting
Feeds: RH report; good/bad matrix (RH and FFWI rows); FAQ
Related questions: DQ1, DQ2, DQ6, DQ7
Relevance: High · Status: Read

Open items: per-model attribution of the RH switch; whether the FFWI=50 threshold is valid for CA; max-wind (vs mean) trends




Q02 — Evaluating Pyregence Synthetic Relative Humidity Product
Cal-Adapt AE 2025 (Will Krantz) · Internal doc · Sec 3
Summary. Evaluation of whether the Pyregence synthetic RH product produces more realistic long-term RH trends.
Key findings. Verdict: acceptable only as a Pyregence wildfire-model input; unacceptable as a standalone or replacement RH product. Applies a roughly uniform negative trend adjustment but FAILS to reproduce ERA5’s strong negative trend when applied to WRF-ERA5. Undocumented training data, undocumented input bias correction, no overfitting validation. Daily-scale artifacts: blotchy spatial patterns, missing inland water, unexplained increases over southern Nevada.
Datasets: UCSD bias-corrected WRF, LOCA2, WRF-ERA5, Pyregence synthetic RH, ERA5 · Variables: RH (daily min/max) · Methods: Trend comparison with 5-yr rolling means; linear trend fitting; regridding to a common grid
Feeds: RH report; data challenges page; cautionary example for the Phase 2 proposal
Related questions: DQ3, DQ5
Relevance: High · Status: Read

Appendix A documents UCLA-WRF vs UCSD post-downscaling bias-corrected WRF differences - useful for provenance flowchart branches




Q03 — LOCA2 wind speed and direction investigation: Original NetCDF files
Cal-Adapt AE 2025 (Ana Ordonez) · Internal doc · Sec 0
Summary. Checks whether wind magnitude derived from components matches the provided wspeed variable.
Key findings. sqrt(uas^2 + vas^2) does not equal wspeed in the original LOCA2 CA hybrid NetCDFs (tested on ACCESS-CM2 ssp245). The discrepancy is identical in the NetCDF and zarr versions, so it is not an AE ingestion issue - it originates upstream.
Datasets: LOCA2 CA hybrid (0.0625deg) · Variables: uas, vas, wspeed · Methods: Direct comparison of derived vs provided wind magnitude; NetCDF vs zarr cross-check
Feeds: Variable cards (uas/vas/wspeed averaging warning); provenance flowchart; data challenges page
Related questions: DQ4
Relevance: High · Status: Read

Hypothesis to verify: wspeed may be the daily mean of sub-daily speed while components are daily means (scalar vs vector averaging). Check whether the difference is one-signed. Note the differing file versions: v20230115 vs v20230901




Q04 — RH Sensitivity Analysis Plan for Cal-Adapt: AE
Cal-Adapt AE 2025 · Internal doc · Sec 2
Summary. The parent plan governing AE’s RH bias work. Defines the goals, a three-tier use-case triage, and three workstreams: historical climatology, Heat Index, and FFWI.
Key findings. Framing document rather than results. Premise: CMIP6 GCMs project more near-surface moisture than observed, likely propagating into downscaled CCA5 data; affects both WRF and LOCA2; errors largest in arid regions and in the hot/dry season. Target output is a three-tier triage of use cases — proceed as-is / adjustment recommended / adjustment critically necessary — plus a feasibility assessment of an actual adjustment procedure. Status: historical climatology and Heat Index not started; FFWI in progress but on hold.
Datasets: WRF, LOCA2 (CCA5), ERA5, HadISD stations, AE airport station locations · Variables: RH, air temperature, dewpoint temperature, Heat Index, FFWI · Methods: Station-based comparison of WRF/LOCA2 vs ERA5 by region and IOU territory; RH derived from HadISD air temp + dewpoint to test a point-based adjustment, then generalized to gridded data; stepwise regional perturbation of RH holding physical consistency with temperature; recalculation of derived metrics (Rothfusz Heat Index, NOAA FFWI) and of threshold/exceedance metrics
Feeds: RH report (parent framing); good/bad matrix — the three-tier triage is the RH row of the matrix; Phase 2 proposal (point→grid generalization); variable cards (RH-dependent derived variables); guidance materials
Related questions: DQ1, DQ3, DQ8, DQ9, DQ10
Relevance: High · Status: Read

Parent plan for Q01 (FFWI). Two of three workstreams not started and one on hold - check current status before building on it. Notes that the equilibrium moisture constant is also used in drought indices, so FFWI findings may transfer. The linked Heat Index slide deck is a separate artifact (see Papers to read).




R20 — Personal communication on LOCA2 CA hybrid wind speed construction
D. Pierce (Scripps), pers. comm., August 2026 [confirm exact date] · Personal communication · Sec 0
Summary. Scripps confirmation of how wspeed is constructed and bias-corrected relative to uas/vas.
Key findings. wspeed is produced by averaging hourly wind speeds to daily (scalar, positive-definite), downscaled and bias-corrected separately from the vector components (signed, can cancel), with different extreme-value handling. Therefore wspeed != sqrt(uas2+vas2) by design. Recommendation: use the downscaled wspeed directly; do not reconstruct from daily vector winds. Resolves DQ4.
Datasets: LOCA2 CA hybrid · Variables: uas, vas, wspeed · Methods: Separate downscaling + bias correction of scalar speed vs vector components
Feeds: wspeed variable card; DQ4 resolution; data challenges page
Related questions: DQ4
Relevance: High · Status: Received

Personal communication; key quote retained in project notes. Fill exact email date.




Q05 — Cal-Adapt downscaled products vs ERA5: 10 m wind agreement over California (v2)
AE internal analysis (H. Inda-Diaz), 2026 · Internal analysis · Sec 1
Summary. Head-to-head validation of AE downscaled 10 m wind (LOCA2 statistical + WRF dynamical, same GCM) vs ERA5 over California, 1980-2010.
Key findings. Both products run high vs ERA5 with agreeing timing (seasonal r 0.77-0.92) and a multiplicative offset. On 1351 shared cells the STATISTICAL LOCA2 (+29%) is CLOSER to ERA5 than the DYNAMICAL WRF-GCM (+69%). This REJECTS the v1 hypothesis that LOCA2’s offset came from PresRat: the uncorrected dynamical product is the outlier and PresRat moves LOCA2 toward ERA5. Offset largest over flat interior terrain (opposite of a resolution effect), so origin is upstream (GCM wind climate, WRF surface/PBL, or ERA5 10m diagnostic at 31km). Big caveat: sampling frequency not matched (WRF native-timestep vs ERA5 hourly) inflates WRF. Decisive next step: WRF-ERA5 run (same sampling).
Datasets: LOCA2 (CNRM-ESM2-1 historical); WRF-GCM (CNRM-ESM2-1 historical); ERA5 · Variables: wspeed / wspd10mean (u10/v10 for ERA5) · Methods: source->ERA5 block-mean regrid (rectilinear + curvilinear paths); coverage mask; ERA5 hourly->scalar->monthly; climatological metrics
Feeds: good/bad matrix (mean-bias dimension); wspeed variable card (ERA5 validation); data challenges page
Related questions: DQ4, DQ9
Relevance: High · Status: Draft

v2 supersedes v1. Single realization each; sampling-frequency caveat on WRF. See era5-comparison page + FINDINGS_v2.md. Next: WRF-ERA5 control run.

title: References
text:
Open questions (DQ##) — details

DQ1
Question. Is the RH trend switch at GWL>=2.5 driven by one model (e.g. TaiESM) or consistent across models?
Raised by: FFWI sensitivity analysis · Datasets: WRF (AE) · Variables: RH
Related sources: Q01, R05, Q04
Status: Open · Priority: High

If it is one model, a possible outcome is an exclusion recommendation for RH and FFWI uses




DQ2
Question. Is FFWI usable at GWL>=2.5, and is the FFWI=50 threshold appropriate for California?
Raised by: FFWI sensitivity analysis · Datasets: WRF (AE) · Variables: FFWI
Related sources: Q01
Status: Open - preliminary caution issued · Priority: High

Feeds the good/bad matrix directly




DQ3
Question. Does WRF downscaling preserve the RH trends of the parent GCM or reanalysis?
Raised by: Pyregence evaluation (WRF-ERA5 vs ERA5 result) · Datasets: WRF-ERA5, WRF-GCM · Variables: RH
Related sources: Q02, R05, Q04, R06, R07, R10
Status: Open · Priority: High

If not, the GCM RH literature may not transfer to downscaled data - this reframes the whole RH report




DQ4
Question. Why does wspeed differ from sqrt(uas^2 + vas^2) in the LOCA2 hybrid files?
Raised by: Ana’s wind investigation · Datasets: LOCA2 CA hybrid · Variables: uas, vas, wspeed
Related sources: Q03, R04, R12, R15, R20
Status: Resolved (Scripps, R20) · Priority: High

RESOLVED: wspeed is a separately downscaled/bias-corrected scalar daily-mean speed, not equal to sqrt(uas2+vas2) by design; use wspeed directly (D. Pierce, Scripps, R20). The positive offset is the scalar pedestal; the left-skewed tail reflects the differing bias correction of speed vs components.




DQ5
Question. What bias correction was applied to the LOCA2 and WRF-ERA5 inputs before synthetic RH generation?
Raised by: Pyregence evaluation · Datasets: LOCA2, WRF-ERA5 · Variables: RH
Related sources: Q02, R06
Status: Open - memo obtained, does not document it · Priority: Medium

The Pyregence memo (R06) has now been read and documents NO additional bias correction on the LOCA2 or WRF-ERA5 inputs. The large LOCA2 bias shift Q02 observed is therefore still unexplained and needs a direct question to the Pyregence team. Related unresolved gap: the memo never names the observational dataset the regression was trained on.




DQ6
Question. Are the projected wind speed decreases robust for maximum winds, not just means?
Raised by: FFWI sensitivity analysis · Datasets: WRF (AE) · Variables: Wind speed
Related sources: Q01, R12
Status: Open · Priority: Medium

Connects to wind pilot Sec 3 - extremes vs means




DQ7
Question. Is the spatial variability of wind and RH trends consistent across GWLs (same areas windier or drier each time)?
Raised by: FFWI sensitivity analysis · Datasets: WRF (AE) · Variables: Wind, RH
Related sources: Q01, R12
Status: Open · Priority: Medium

Flagged as to-be-determined in the source doc




DQ8
Question. Is the RH bias constant in time, or does it change over the projection period?
Raised by: RH Sensitivity Analysis Plan (Q04) · Datasets: WRF, LOCA2 (CCA5) · Variables: RH
Related sources: Q04, R06, R07
Status: Open · Priority: High

Determines whether a single-offset correction is even viable. Direct input to the Phase 2 proposal.




DQ9
Question. Can a station-derived RH adjustment (HadISD dewpoint-derived RH) be generalised from points to the full grid?
Raised by: RH Sensitivity Analysis Plan (Q04) · Datasets: WRF, LOCA2, HadISD stations · Variables: RH, dewpoint temperature
Related sources: Q04, R16, R18
Status: Open · Priority: High

This is the full-grid bias adjustment question in RH form - the same problem as the Phase 2 wind proposal, and the sparse-station difficulty is shared. Strong case for scoping the two together.




DQ10
Question. Which AE derived variables and metrics depend on RH?
Raised by: RH Sensitivity Analysis Plan (Q04) · Datasets: WRF, LOCA2 · Variables: RH, Heat Index, FFWI, derived RH
Related sources: Q04, Q01, R10
Status: Open · Priority: High

Named so far: Heat Index, FFWI and ‘derived RH’. Confirm the complete list. Pure documentation, answerable now, feeds the variable cards directly.




DQ11
Question. Is the memo’s claim correct that bias correction can fix mean and variance but not long-term trend errors? If so, what does that imply for the Phase 2 full-grid method choice?
Raised by: Pyregence memo (R06) · Datasets: WRF, LOCA2 · Variables: RH, and any variable with a suspect trend
Related sources: R06, R07, R05, R09, R13, R14, R17, R19
Status: Open · Priority: High

This is the most load-bearing methodological claim we have found for Phase 2. If true as stated, quantile-mapping-family methods cannot fix the RH problem and the shortlist must centre on trend-preserving or trend-correcting approaches - or concede that a rebuild (as Pyregence chose) is the only option. Note the claim is asserted in a draft memo, not demonstrated, so it needs testing against the bias-correction literature rather than adoption.
